name: Egalitarianism
summary: Egalitarianism makes equality the chief value of a just society. It starts from the equal worth of every person, then demands that institutions narrow undeserved inequalities of wealth, opportunity and power, either by equalising some good (resources, welfare, capabilities) or by abolishing hierarchies of status and domination. Most egalitarians reject strict equality of outcomes and stay committed to extensive liberal rights.
scope: The mainstream of contemporary egalitarian political philosophy as the Stanford entries present it (Rawls's liberal egalitarianism, luck and resource egalitarians such as Dworkin and Sen's capability approach, and relational egalitarians such as Anderson), plus Tawney's Equality as the classic egalitarian socialist text. Answers rest on what these sources state about equal worth, legal and political equality, equal opportunity and redistribution; generic liberal-democratic positions, and Marxist, anarchist or religious equality movements as such, are not borrowed.
